original_claim: 75% of Indonesian trucks are single-vehicle owner-operators (~1.3M trucks)
verdict_summary: The 75% figure exists in primary literature but describes a different metric. World Bank (2015) found that 'over 75% of trucking companies at Tanjung Priok have 20 or fewer trucks' — i.e., 75% of companies are small-fleet operators, not 75% of trucks are single-vehicle owner-operators. A separate World Bank (2016) study found 'operators that own 1 to 5 trucks account for the majority of companies, but only handle a small portion of trucks.' The original claim conflates company count with truck count and overstates the single-vehicle threshold. The total registered truck count per BPS 2023 is ~6.1 million, not ~1.3 million used in the original claim.
verified_value: Over 75% of trucking companies operating at Tanjung Priok (Indonesia's main container port) have 20 or fewer trucks. Operators owning 1–5 trucks constitute the majority of companies by count but handle only a small share of total truck volume. The trucking sector has over 1 million registered companies (World Bank 2016), concentrated in small operators. Total registered trucks: ~6.1 million (BPS 2023). No primary source confirms '75% of trucks are single-vehicle owner-operators' as a share of the total fleet.

best_source.key_quote: The trucking market is very fragmented. An analysis of the structure of the companies that perform the trucking services in Tanjung Priok shows that over 75% of the companies have 20 or less trucks.

supporting_sources.key_quote: The Indonesian trucking sector is fragmented with over 1 million trucking companies (World Bank, 2016). Smaller operators that own 1 to 5 trucks account for the majority of the companies, but only handle a small portion of trucks (World Bank, 2016).
supporting_sources.note: Cites World Bank 2016 for both the 1 million companies figure and the 1-5 truck majority-of-companies finding. That World Bank 2016 document is: 'The Republic of Indonesia Study on Trade in Logistics Services Analysis' (7 December 2016), accessed at documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/232691540822189989/pdf/Analysis.pdf — PDF conversion returned garbled output; content confirmed via GIZ citation chain.

supporting_sources.title: OECD Competition Assessment Reviews: Logistics Sector in ASEAN
supporting_sources.key_quote: The ASEAN freight and logistics market remains fragmented, with a mix of major international and local operators. Some member states, such as Indonesia and the Philippines, have a large number of local players.
supporting_sources.note: OECD ASEAN-wide report cites Mordor Intelligence (a commercial aggregator) for market-size data; does not itself publish the 75% owner-operator claim. Confirms fleet fragmentation qualitatively.

Total fleet size confirms the '~1.3 million' in the original claim is incorrect — total registered trucks are ~6.1 million, not 1.3 million. The 1.3 million figure may refer to something else (perhaps unique operators, or an older/narrower count). recommendation: Replace text in Pain Point 1.4 with: 'Indonesia's trucking market is highly fragmented: over 75% of trucking companies operating at Tanjung Priok port have fleets of 20 trucks or fewer, and operators owning just 1–5 trucks make up the majority of registered companies — though they handle only a small share of total freight volume [World Bank, 2015]. With more than 1 million registered trucking companies [World Bank, 2016] and a total fleet of ~6.1 million trucks [BPS, 2023], individual small operators face severe capital constraints on fleet renewal, fuel purchasing, and digital adoption.' Remove the original '75% are single-vehicle owner-operators (~1.3M trucks)' language, which conflates company count (75% of companies have ≤20 trucks) with individual truck ownership share, and uses an incorrect total fleet figure. Cite: [A] World Bank (2015), Improving Indonesia's Freight Logistics System, p.17; [B] GIZ/Changing-Transport (2021), Truck Fleet Modernization in Indonesia, citing World Bank (2016); [C] BPS (2023), Jumlah Kendaraan Bermotor.
